subject: fixture-science
text: A reaction statement lists the starting materials on the left and what is formed on the right. The arrow in the middle is read as changes into. The number written before a formula tells how many units of that substance take part, so a statement can be balanced by counting the atoms of each element on both sides.

subject: fixture-science
text: Silver chloride is a pale white solid that turns grey when it is left in sunlight. Light supplies the energy that splits it into silver metal, which looks grey, and chlorine gas, which escapes into the air. Photographers once used this change to make pictures on paper coated with silver salts.

subject: fixture-science
text: A similar light-driven change happens in green leaves, but far more slowly and under the control of pigments. Energy from sunlight is stored in the bonds of the sugar that the leaf builds, and the oxygen that is released comes from water rather than from the carbon dioxide the leaf takes in.

subject: fixture-science
text: Water in which red cabbage has been boiled is a home-made indicator. It turns pink in a sour liquid and green-blue in a soapy one. Turmeric paste behaves in the opposite way: it stays yellow in sour liquids and turns red-brown in soapy ones.

subject: fixture-maths
text: A statement of the form a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero has at most two solutions. The solutions can be read from the graph as the points where the curve crosses the horizontal axis. When the curve does not cross that axis at all, the statement has no real solutions.

subject: fixture-maths
text: The distance between two points on a grid is found by treating the difference in the horizontal coordinates and the difference in the vertical coordinates as the two shorter sides of a right triangle, and then applying the relation between the sides of that triangle.
